disease_info: Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type) is characterized by an uninterrupted period of illness during which there is a major depressive episode concurrent with Criterion A symptoms of schizophrenia (such as delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking, grossly disorganized behavior, and negative symptoms). To meet criteria, there must also be at least two weeks of psychotic symptoms occurring in the absence of prominent mood symptoms, distinguishing it from mood disorders with psychotic features. Over time, individuals often show fluctuating intensity of mood and psychotic features, with significant impairment in social and occupational functioning. Compared with schizophrenia, mood symptoms are more prominent and enduring; compared with major depressive disorder with psychotic features, psychosis is more autonomous and not confined strictly to mood episodes.

narrative.personality: Jose is warm, sociable, and deeply community-oriented, with a meticulous yet sometimes overcommitted approach to organizing cultural events and nurturing neighborhood connections.
narrative.stressor: Over the past two years, Jose had been trying to turn his informal community organizing and event coordination into a more formal role with the public library while also planning a home-based catering business, all against the backdrop of limited formal education and being out of the traditional workforce for years. As grant applications, municipal paperwork, and expectations from the library accumulated, he became increasingly overwhelmed by the administrative demands and the sense that this was his last chance to secure stable recognition for his work. He began sleeping less, withdrawing from some of his usual salsa nights and senior center reading sessions, and spending long, disorganized hours trying to juggle project planning, permits, and family expectations, which gradually eroded his confidence and day-to-day functioning over more than a year. He finally sought psychiatric care when his planning conversations with collaborators became so tangential and confusing that meetings repeatedly fell apart, community members expressed concern, and he realized he could no longer reliably coordinate even small neighborhood events.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately when I try to explain my ideas or plan an event, my thoughts get all jumbled and I can’t talk in a straight line.”

narrative.personality: Jiyeon is driven, detail-oriented, and competitive, balancing a high-achieving scientific mindset with an active social and fitness-focused lifestyle.
narrative.stressor: About a year and a half before presentation, Jiyeon experienced a prolonged period of unexplained fatigue and minor health complaints, leading to several inconclusive medical evaluations that heightened her tendency toward worry and self-scrutiny. At the same time, her lab was undergoing restructuring, and she took on extra responsibilities to prove herself for a supervisory role, pushing through her physical exhaustion and neglecting rest and recreation. Over months, her sense of physical vulnerability and fear of having a serious undiagnosed illness blended with mounting stress at work, and she became increasingly preoccupied, withdrawn from her usual hiking and soccer, and less able to organize her thoughts during quality-improvement meetings and mentoring sessions. She eventually sought psychiatric help after colleagues and friends noticed that her once-clear explanations and presentations had become scattered and confusing, and she herself felt unable to trust her own thinking while worrying that her health issues meant she was “falling apart.”
narrative.chief_complaint: “My thoughts feel all over the place, and when I try to explain something at work, I lose my train of thought and can’t make it make sense.”

narrative.personality: Myriam is creative, introspective, and community-minded, with a relaxed but sometimes disorganized approach to school and projects, and a deep interest in using art to tell cultural stories.
narrative.stressor: Myriam’s difficulties emerged shortly after she moved from her familiar neighborhood to start college, juggling a new campus environment, looser structure, and the expectation to turn her artistic passion into a viable path. Initially excited, she soon felt overwhelmed by managing deadlines, navigating financial aid, and living away from her close-knit family, which clashed with her naturally laid-back and somewhat disorganized style. Over the next year, she began skipping classes, spending long, unfocused stretches on half-finished digital illustrations and community-themed projects while feeling increasingly isolated and uncertain about her future, and her conversations with peers and instructors became harder to follow as her thoughts wandered and failed to connect. She ultimately came to psychiatric attention after professors expressed concern about a dramatic decline in her academic performance and studio participation and her family noticed that even simple conversations about daily plans or coursework had become fragmented and confusing for her to get through.
narrative.chief_complaint: “When I try to talk about my ideas or school stuff, my thoughts get mixed up and I can’t keep a clear line, so people say they can’t follow me.”
